questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young male seeking to study abroad has a chest X-ray taken for immigration purposes, which reveals air beneath both domes of the diaphragm. He shows no symptoms and has normal vital signs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis

The given clinical scenario with an asymptomatic patient having air under the diaphragm without evidence of peritonitis (sterile pneumoperitoneum) is suggestive of pneumatosis intestinalis.

Pneumatosis Intestinalis presents as multiple gas filled cysts of the gastrointestinal tract. Most common site is jejunum>ileocecal region >colon. It has Equal incidence among males and females and it most commonly occurs in the 4th-7th decades of life. Pneumatosis in neonates is usually associated with necrotizing enterocolitis. The histiopathological finding shows a honeycomb appearance with thin walled cyst ehich break easily and spontaneous rupture of cyst give rise to pneumoperitoneum.

Clinical features are mostly nonspecific,most commonly diarrhea, abdominal pain, abdominal distention, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, and mucus in stools. Diagnosis on plain films is radiolucent areas within the bowel wall (appear as grape-like clusters or tiny bubbles) and alternatively, barium contrast or CT studies can be used to confirm the diagnosis.

Treatment include, management of the uncomplicated primary disease and when symptoms demand treatment, the first line is intermittent high flow oxygen therapy, providing a concentration of 70% continuously for 5 days by nasal specula. The cysts may also resolve with antibiotics, particularly metronidazole and in resistant cases, maintenance treatment with sulfasalazine may be helpful.

The image given below is the plain xray showing air under diaphragm and radiolucent areas within the bowel wall.

Other options :

Option b : Diverticulitis on CT abdomen shows bright bowel outpouching, which may be complicated by infection and abscess formation.

Option c : In Peptic ulcer perforation, the supine abdominal x-ray shows air beneath the diaphragm along with Rigler's double-wall sign indicating pneumoperitoneum, as shown in the image given below. Consumption of alcohol and chronic tobacco smoking are high-risk factors for developing peptic ulcers. Fever and tachycardia suggest peritonitis from the perforated ulcer.

Option d : Duodenal atresia is caused by the failure of vacuolization of the solid duodenum. It is commonly seen in newborns with Down’s syndrome. Babies usually present with bilious vomiting immediately after birth. A plain X-ray abdomen reveals two foci of gas, one in the stomach and the other in the duodenum called the double bubble sign (as shown below).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient complaining of pain in the right flank has been diagnosed with right-sided renal calculi measuring 2.2cm. Urine microscopy findings are shown in the image below. What is the most suitable treatment for this patient?
options: No treatment required just pain management suffices
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy

The image of the urine microscopy shows hexagonal-shaped cystine stones. Hence the best suitable treatment for this patient with cysteine renal calculi measuring 2.2 cm is percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL).

Cysteine stone is relatively resistant to extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy and a stone size of more than 2 cm necessitates percutaneous nephrolithotomy. Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy is done until the renal stone size of less than 1.5cm.

PCNL is indicated in the following condition:

• If the patient has anatomical obstruction like pelviureteric junction obstruction, calyceal diverticula, or distal ureteral obstruction.
• Hard renal stones like cystine stones, and calcium oxalate stones.
• If the renal stone is struvite stone as it is associated with urinary tract infection.

Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) is a non-invasive method that generates shockwaves outside the body, which are focused on the stones. It is the commonest method of treating urinary tract stones nowadays. Stones up to approximately 1.5 cm in size are suitable for this form of treatment.

Complications of ESWL include infection, haematuria, parenchymal hemorrhage, and perirenal hematoma. ESWL is contraindicated in obese patients, pregnant patients, and patients taking oral anticoagulants.

Note: Stone fragments collected in the distal ureter following ESWL are called steinstrasse.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old male patient involved in a road traffic accident was brought unconscious to the emergency room. CT brain reveals the following findings. All of the following are indications for performing an open craniotomy in this patient except?
options: A GCS drop of 6 points in a comatose patient
A GCS drop of 4 points in a comatose patient
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Midline shift of 3 mm

The above clinical scenario and the plain computed tomography (CT) scan shows a concavo-convex-shaped hematoma on the left side suggestive of an acute subdural hematoma (SDH). A midline shift > 5mm is considered an indication for performing an open craniotomy.

Acute SDH results from the accumulation of blood between the arachnoid membrane and the dura. The tearing of a bridging vein running from the cerebral cortex to the dural sinuses is the most common cause of acute SDH.

On head CT scan, acute SDH appears as a hyperdense, crescent-shaped (concavo-convex) lesion (as seen in this question)

Open craniotomy for the evacuation of acute SDH is indicated for the following:

1. Thickness >1 cm
2. Midline shift >5 mm

Emergent decompression is also recommended to a comatose patient with an acute subdural hematoma less than 1 cm in thickness causing a midline shift of less than 5 mm if any of the following criteria are met:

•  GCS drops by two or more points from the time of injury to the hospitalization
•  The patient presents with fixed and dilated pupils
• ICP is >20mm Hg
